Before addressing the question of omissions, consider a related issue 
of ambiguity. When parties reach a deal, their agreement is expressed in 
words. But words are only imperfect proxies for the ideas they represent. 
Sometimes the words used by the parties admit more than one meaning; 
for example, a word may have one meaning in general discourse and a 
special meaning in a particular business context. When a transaction has 
been reduced to writing and a dispute arises as to the meaning of what 
has been written down, should a court simply do its best to mterpret the 
writing on its own? Or may the parties assist the court by providing

agreement, it was included in the agreement even though 1t was never 
written or perhaps even expressed orally? The problem here is not 
differing assertions of the meaning of words used by the parties but, 
rather, differing assertions about matters that were implici in the "deal" 
but never reduced to words. How does the law deal with su h disputes?
